lessonTitle: First-Order and Zero-Order Elimination: Linear and Saturable Kinetics

blocks.text: Two friends drink the same amount of alcohol, but the one who drinks twice as fast stays intoxicated far longer than twice as long. The liver enzyme that handles alcohol works at its maximum speed, so extra alcohol simply waits its turn. A few important drugs behave the same way, with dangerous consequences when the dose is nudged upwards.

blocks.markdown: Most drugs are eliminated by **first-order** kinetics: the rate of elimination is proportional to the plasma concentration, so a constant **fraction** of drug is removed per unit time. Some drugs, at some concentrations, show **zero-order** (saturable) kinetics: the elimination enzymes or transporters are working at their maximum, so a constant **amount** of drug is removed per unit time, whatever the concentration.

blocks.title: First-order and zero-order elimination
blocks.text: First-order: elimination rate = k x C, so a constant fraction is eliminated per unit time, the half-life is constant, and a plot of log concentration against time is a straight line. Zero-order: elimination rate is constant (it equals Vmax, the maximum rate), a constant amount is removed per unit time, there is no constant half-life, and a plot of concentration against time is a straight line.

blocks.caption: Michaelis-Menten elimination. Vmax = maximum elimination rate (mg/day); Km = concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax (mg/L). When C is much smaller than Km, the rate is approximately (Vmax/Km) x C, which is first order; when C is much larger than Km, the rate approaches Vmax, which is zero order.

blocks.title: Comparing first-order and zero-order removal
blocks.prompt: A patient has 80 mg of Drug F (first order, 25% eliminated per hour) and 80 mg of Drug Z (zero order, 10 mg eliminated per hour) in the body. Compare the amounts remaining over the next three hours. (Teaching example.)

steps.text: Drug F: each hour 25% of the current amount is removed, so 75% remains. After 1 h: 80 x 0.75 = 60 mg. After 2 h: 60 x 0.75 = 45 mg. After 3 h: 45 x 0.75 = 33.75 mg.
Drug Z: each hour a fixed 10 mg is removed. After 1 h: 70 mg. After 2 h: 60 mg. After 3 h: 50 mg.
Note the pattern: the amount of F removed each hour falls (20, 15, 11.25 mg) because the concentration falls; the amount of Z removed stays the same (10 mg).
Consequence: for Z the time to eliminate depends on the starting amount, so there is no fixed half-life; the 80 mg takes 8 h, whereas 160 mg would take 16 h.

blocks.answer: F: 60, 45, 33.75 mg; Z: 70, 60, 50 mg; F loses a constant fraction, Z a constant amount.

blocks.caption: First-order versus zero-order elimination.
rows: Disproportionate; small dose rise can cause a large level rise
Ethanol; phenytoin (near therapeutic range); high-dose aspirin; at toxic doses, others

blocks.markdown: **Phenytoin.** Phenytoin's hepatic metabolism approaches saturation within its therapeutic range (conventionally about 10 to 20 mg/L, which varies by laboratory and by protein binding). At steady state, input rate R equals elimination rate, so rearranging the Michaelis-Menten equation gives the steady-state concentration. Because R sits in both the numerator and the denominator term (Vmax minus R), as R approaches Vmax the concentration climbs very steeply.

blocks.caption: R = dosing rate (mg/day). Css rises without bound as R approaches Vmax, which is why no steady state is reached if R is greater than or equal to Vmax.

blocks.title: Why phenytoin levels rise disproportionately
blocks.prompt: A patient has Vmax = 500 mg/day and Km = 5 mg/L for phenytoin (teaching values). Calculate the steady-state concentration at doses of 300, 400 and 450 mg/day.

steps.text: A 33% dose increase from 300 to 400 mg/day raised the level 2.7-fold, and a further 12.5% increase more than doubled it again. The enzyme is near its maximum, so extra drug cannot be cleared faster and accumulates.

blocks.answer: 7.5, 20 and 45 mg/L: a small increase in dose causes a disproportionate rise in level

blocks.title: Dosing saturable drugs
blocks.text: Increase doses of phenytoin in small steps and re-check the level after steady state, because a modest rise in dose can move a level from therapeutic to toxic (nystagmus, ataxia, confusion).

blocks.markdown: **Renal impairment.** For drugs eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney, clearance falls in proportion to glomerular filtration rate (GFR). The maintenance dose rate must fall or the dosing interval must lengthen, otherwise the drug accumulates. A loading dose is usually unaffected because it depends on Vd. A common approach is to calculate a dose factor from the fraction of the drug excreted unchanged in the urine (fe) and the patient's GFR relative to normal.

blocks.caption: fe = fraction excreted unchanged in urine (0 to 1). The adjusted maintenance dose = usual dose x dose factor. If fe is small the factor remains near 1 and little adjustment is needed.

items: Renally cleared drugs needing adjustment include gentamicin, digoxin, lithium, many beta-lactam antibiotics and metformin.
Options: reduce each dose, lengthen the interval, or both; use drug level monitoring for narrow therapeutic index drugs.
Estimated GFR (or creatinine clearance) is used to decide the adjustment, with formulae varying by drug and reference source.
Older adults often have reduced GFR even when serum creatinine looks normal because of low muscle mass.

blocks.title: Zero-order accumulation
blocks.text: With a saturable drug, doubling the dose can more than double the level, and the time to lower the level after an overdose is prolonged because the half-life lengthens as concentration rises.

points: First-order elimination removes a constant fraction per unit time with a fixed half-life; zero-order removes a constant amount because elimination is saturated.
Phenytoin and ethanol show saturable kinetics, so small dose increases can cause disproportionate rises in plasma level (Css = Km x R / (Vmax - R)).
In renal impairment, drugs eliminated renally accumulate unless the dose or interval is adjusted according to GFR and the fraction excreted unchanged.

options.text: A constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time
A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time
The half-life increases as concentration rises
Elimination stops at therapeutic concentrations

questions.correctOptionText: A constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the rate is proportional to concentration.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: half-life is constant in first-order kinetics.

questions.explanation: In first-order kinetics the rate of elimination is proportional to the concentration, so the same fraction is removed each time period. The half-life is therefore constant.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old is brought to the emergency department after drinking heavily. His blood ethanol falls at a roughly constant rate of the same number of milligrams per decilitre each hour. Which kinetic behaviour does this show?

options.text: Zero-order elimination, because the enzyme system is saturated
First-order elimination, because the enzymes are not saturated
Elimination by exhalation only
Renal elimination of unchanged ethanol

questions.correctOptionText: Zero-order elimination, because the enzyme system is saturated

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a constant amount is removed per unit time as alcohol dehydrogenase works at maximum capacity.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: first-order would show a falling absolute rate as concentration falls.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: only a minor fraction is exhaled.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: most ethanol is metabolised in the liver.

questions.explanation: At typical intoxicating concentrations the enzymes metabolising ethanol are saturated, so removal proceeds at a fixed maximum rate. This gives a linear fall in concentration with time, characteristic of zero-order kinetics.

questions.stem: A patient has Vmax = 600 mg/day and Km = 4 mg/L for phenytoin (teaching values). Using Css = Km x R / (Vmax - R), calculate the steady-state concentration in mg/L at a dosing rate R of 450 mg/day.
questions.explanation: Css = 4 x 450 / (600 - 450) = 1800 / 150 = 12 mg/L. Raising R to 500 mg/day would give 4 x 500 / 100 = 20 mg/L, so an 11% dose increase would raise the level by two-thirds.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with epilepsy has a phenytoin level of 8 mg/L on 300 mg daily and seizures continue. Her prescriber raises the dose to 400 mg daily and the next steady-state level is 25 mg/L, with nystagmus and ataxia. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Phenytoin metabolism is saturable, so near capacity a small dose rise produces a large rise in concentration
The drug is eliminated by first-order kinetics, so level should have risen by exactly 33%
Phenytoin bioavailability increases with dose
Phenytoin induces its own renal excretion

questions.correctOptionText: Phenytoin metabolism is saturable, so near capacity a small dose rise produces a large rise in concentration

distractorRationale.a: Correct: near saturation, extra dose cannot be cleared proportionally and accumulates.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: first-order kinetics would give proportional change, which did not occur.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: bioavailability is not the explanation.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: phenytoin is mainly cleared by hepatic metabolism.

questions.explanation: The observed 3-fold rise from a 33% dose increase is the hallmark of Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Her enzyme capacity is close to saturated, so levels climb steeply and toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia) emerges.

questions.stem: Explain why phenytoin shows disproportionate rises in plasma level after small dose increases, and how this should influence prescribing.
markingGuide: Hepatic metabolising enzymes become saturated within or near the therapeutic range
Elimination changes from first order to zero order, approaching a maximum rate Vmax
At steady state input = elimination, Css = Km x R / (Vmax - R), so Css rises steeply as R approaches Vmax
Half-life also lengthens as the concentration rises
Prescribing: increase in small increments, check levels at steady state (which may take days to weeks), watch for toxicity such as nystagmus and ataxia
questions.explanation: Because enzyme capacity is limited, the clearance falls as concentration rises, so accumulation accelerates. This makes dose changes unpredictable without monitoring.

questions.stem: A drug has fe = 0.9 (90% excreted unchanged by the kidneys) and the usual maintenance dose is 1000 mg per day. A patient has a GFR that is 30% of the normal value. Using Dose factor = 1 - fe x (1 - GFR ratio), calculate the adjusted daily dose in mg. (Teaching example.)
questions.explanation: GFR ratio = 0.3, so 1 - 0.3 = 0.7 and fe x 0.7 = 0.63. Dose factor = 1 - 0.63 = 0.37, so the dose is 0.37 x 1000 = 370 mg/day.

questions.stem: Which approach is appropriate for a drug that is mainly excreted unchanged by the kidneys in a patient with reduced eGFR?

options.text: Reduce the maintenance dose or lengthen the dosing interval, and monitor levels if the drug has a narrow therapeutic index
Increase the dose to compensate for reduced effect
No change, since renal function never affects drug levels
Switch to a loading dose daily

questions.correctOptionText: Reduce the maintenance dose or lengthen the dosing interval, and monitor levels if the drug has a narrow therapeutic index

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lower clearance requires lower input to avoid accumulation.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: this would cause accumulation and toxicity.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: renal function strongly affects renally cleared drugs.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: repeated loading would cause toxicity.

questions.explanation: Reduced GFR lowers clearance of a renally excreted drug, so the maintenance dose that was appropriate for normal function leads to accumulation. Adjusting dose or interval restores the target exposure.

questions.stem: Describe how renal impairment alters the dosing of renally cleared drugs, giving two examples of drugs requiring adjustment.
markingGuide: Renal clearance falls in proportion to GFR, so elimination is slower and half-life lengthens
Without adjustment the drug accumulates, risking toxicity
Adjust by reducing maintenance dose and/or extending interval, based on eGFR/creatinine clearance and fe
Loading dose usually unchanged as it depends on Vd
Examples: gentamicin, digoxin, lithium, metformin, many beta-lactams; monitor levels for narrow therapeutic index drugs
questions.explanation: Maintenance dosing must match clearance, which falls when GFR falls. Failure to adjust leads to accumulation and avoidable toxicity.

questions.stem: On a graph of log plasma concentration against time, which elimination pattern gives a straight line?

options.text: First-order elimination
Zero-order elimination
Both patterns give the same line
Neither pattern gives a straight line

distractorRationale.a: Correct: exponential decay is linear on a log axis.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: zero-order gives a straight line on a linear concentration axis.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: first-order is straight on a log plot.

questions.explanation: A constant fraction removed per unit time gives exponential decay, which becomes linear when concentration is plotted on a logarithmic scale. Zero-order removal is linear on a normal axis.

questions.stem: True or false: in zero-order elimination a constant fraction of the drug is removed per unit time.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: In zero-order elimination a constant amount is removed per unit time because the elimination process is saturated. A constant fraction is the property of first-order elimination.
